newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--New home sales, more Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--New home sales, more Greenspan.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market probably faces a moderate volume session with a downward bias on Tuesday, market analysts said.

"The (economic) numbers we'll be getting are minor in nature," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "Given that, I don't think we would see a big move in prices. If we see any move at all, I would tend to think the negative tone that was evident last week and again on Monday might push prices slightly lower."
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond finished lower on Monday, down 12/32 to 97-11/32 to yield 6.83 percent.
"Volume was light on Monday and I don't think you're going to see a lot of volume (on Tuesday) either," said Mary Dennis, senior market economist at Credit Suisse First Boston.

"The economic numbers we're getting before the (February) payroll report (on Friday) and ahead of the second leg of the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony (on Wednesday) aren't that meaningful," said Dennis. "You could see a little bit of bottom fishing at these levels, but with most people pretty bearish, I don't see prices going too much higher," she said.

Several second-tier economic reports are on tap for Tuesday. In addition, Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan will testify before the House Budget Committee on the federal budget and the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

Two weekly surveys on chain and department store sales are scheduled -- the BTM/Schroders survey at 0900 EST/1400 GMT and the Redbook survey at 1455 EST/1955 GMT. Both cover the week ended March 1. The BTM/Schroders survey was down 0.3 percent in the week ended February 22 while the Redbook report was up 0.1 percent. No forecasts were available for the latest week.
"The Mitsubishi number will matter in the morning when we get in," said Dennis. "It's usually floating out there in the market before it's officially released."
Market participants are interested in readings on consumer behavior, said Dennis.
"The retail sector definitely is important," she said. "We've seen a lot of strong numbers lately and first quarter consumption growth is shaping up to be pretty solid from what we've seen."
The Conference Board's Leading Economic Indicators Index, due at 1000 EST/1500 GMT, will be a non-event, traders said.
The index is expected to be up 0.5 percent for January, after a 0.1 percent December increase.
New homes sales figures for January, also due at 1000 EST/1500 GMT, will interest the market more, analysts said.
New home sales slipped to an annualized 757,000 in January from 783,000 in December, according to an average estimate gathered in a Reuters poll.
"Most of the forecasts I've seen are for a small change," said Moran. "If we get that, it should not be a big market mover, but a sizable change could have some influence."

All the day's events will be set against the expectations of another session of Congressional testimony by Fed Chairman Greenspan on the economy on Wednesday and the release of the February U.S. payroll report on Friday.
Also, if the dollar were to weaken, that might intensify the market's negative tone, said Moran.
"Customers will probably remain a bit on the cautious side ahead of Wednesday and Friday," said Dennis.
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open between 5-1/4 percent and 5-3/16 percent on Tuesday.
